analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination in health care and lets patients file complaints and sue providers for unequal treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Padilla with one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate HELP Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for health care providers to give patients worse care based on race, national origin, sex, disability, age, or religion. It would require federal health agencies to collect patient-outcome data broken down by race and other demographics, create an administrative complaint process at HHS with investigations and mediation, and let patients sue providers in court for actual and punitive damages. It would also rename HHS's civil rights office, stand up a permanent Federal Health Equity Commission, add equity measures to Medicare's hospital payment program, allow exclusion of providers from Medicare and Medicaid for a pattern of inequitable care, and give hospitals grants for bias training and translation services.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who receive lower-quality care because of who they are — the bill's findings cite National Academy of Medicine evidence that racial and ethnic minorities receive worse care even with comparable insurance, income, and condition. It gives them a formal complaint process, a federal investigation with deadlines, and a private right of action with damages and attorney's fees, plus new demographic data that would make disparities visible.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits health care providers from subjecting individuals to inequitable care on the basis of race, national origin, sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity), disability, age, or religion, and requires HHS to notify patients of these rights.

It creates an administrative complaint process: patients file within one year, HHS must investigate within 180 days, providers must answer, and the agency pursues conciliation, with reports sent to state licensing boards.

Patients can sue in federal or state court for actual and punitive damages, injunctions, and attorney's fees, and the Attorney General can bring pattern-or-practice suits with punitive damages up to $500,000 for a first violation and $1,000,000 for subsequent ones.

It requires providers to report health outcome data disaggregated by race, national origin, sex, disability, and age, and to store it in a federal repository without individually identifiable information, so patterns of inequitable care can be detected.
It lets HHS exclude a provider from Medicare and Medicaid for a pattern of inequitable care, though with an exception where exclusion would reduce access for underserved or low-income communities.

It ties Medicare's hospital value-based purchasing payments to equitable-care measures beginning in fiscal 2025 and authorizes grants to hospitals for bias training, translation services, diverse workforce recruitment, and outcome tracking, prioritizing hospitals serving low-income patients.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health care providers bear the cost of demographic data reporting, complaint investigations, conciliation, potential lawsuits with punitive damages, and possible Medicare or Medicaid exclusion. Taxpayers fund the renamed civil rights office, the new commission, and the hospital grant program, all left to annual appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition of an inequitable provision of health care is broad — failing a 'high-quality care standard' plus discrimination 'in intent or effect' — which could expose providers to complaints and litigation over patient outcomes that stem from poverty, housing, or other factors outside the provider's control, even though the bill directs investigators to account for such social determinants.

The new complaint, investigation, commission, and grant systems are authorized without dedicated funding beyond annual appropriations, and the bill sets detailed procedural deadlines that would require significant administrative capacity at HHS.

The Medicare exclusion threat is softened by an exception: HHS cannot exclude a provider if that would make it harder for underserved or low-income communities to get care, which limits the remedy exactly where discriminatory-care patterns may be most common.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing documented disparities in care, the bill offers real tools — data transparency, a complaint process, and court access with fee-shifting that makes suits financially feasible. The costs are compliance burdens on hospitals and new federal spending, and the enforcement design is deliberately cautious: it accounts for social determinants of health, requires a pattern rather than a single incident, and restricts exclusion where it would cut off access. The main weakness is that a law this dependent on federal investigative capacity could underdeliver if not funded.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it died without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Alex Padilla introduced S. 4065, the Equal Health Care for All Act, in the Senate on March 22, 2024.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; that referral is the last action in the bill's history.
The bill drew a single cosponsor, Sen. Cory Booker, and never advanced to a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care providers, who avoided new demographic reporting requirements, federal complaint investigations, damages exposure, and possible Medicare exclusion; no patient gained any protection from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, citing health inequity in Black communities and the need to prohibit bias in health care delivery.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Bernard Sanders)
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the March 22, 2024 referral — no hearing, no markup, no report — so the bill never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill drew no floor action that would have revealed a wider partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would expose providers to demographic data reporting, civil rights complaint investigations, patient lawsuits with punitive damages, and possible Medicare or Medicaid exclusion, while also offering them grants for bias training, translation, and workforce diversity. Providers' institutional interest in avoiding liability and payment penalties runs against the bill's patient-protection purpose, though the exclusion carve-out for underserved communities limits the harshest consequence.

industries.industry: Federal health agencies (HHS and its civil rights apparatus)
industries.note: The bill renames the Office for Civil Rights as the Office for Civil Rights and Health Equity with a presidentially appointed director, and creates a permanent Federal Health Equity Commission with subpoena power and annual appropriations — a significant expansion of the agency's mandate and budget.
